text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- New niche banks are attracting customers away from Sweden's traditional banks. Some 300,000 Swedes have transferred their savings to small banks over the past two years.

- Drug use is on the rise among Swedish youths. Alcohol consumption among pupils in the final year of compulsory school is falling while more than twice as many young people say they have tried drugs compared to 1991.
- Sweden will be more dependent on electricity produced from fossil fuels because dry weather has caused water levels in hydro-electric power resevoirs to fall.

- Astra is to launch a drug against impotence which will be available in Sweden in 1997. European sales of the drug, developed by U.S. research company Vivus, are estimated at 500 million crowns annually.
- Stockholm city administration says it will not follow other local authorities in lowering welfare payments, saying families with children would suffer too much.
- A fall in unemployment is on the horizon. One in four small companies says it is planning to hire personnel, a survey shows.
- The average annual salary in Sweden fell by 5,000 crowns to 111,000 crowns between 1990 and 1995, a report by the Swedish employers' confederation shows.
- Labour Minister Margareta Winberg inaugurates a private employment agency, but says it will not be an alternative to the state's own job agencies.
- Volvo aims to sell 500,000 cars per year by the end of the decade, helped by investments in 10 new models.
